What lies at the
heart of an ice giant?
Imagine diving straight
down into the heart
of Neptune, leaving the
wispy methane clouds behind.
As you plunge deeper,
the pressure climbs to
many thousands of times
that of Earth’s atmosphere
at sea level.
The temperature rises
rapidly, turning the
surrounding hydrogen and
helium gas into a
superheated, dense
supercritical fluid.
Beneath this thick gaseous
shroud lies, according
to models, a vast,
crushing ocean that
astronomers call the
planetary mantle.
But do not picture
liquid water like our
calm earthly seas.
This mantle is thought
to be a churning,
super-dense slush of water,
ammonia, and methane,
heated to thousands of
degrees yet kept from
boiling by monstrous
pressures.
Molecules of methane,
composed of carbon and
hydrogen atoms, begin to
break apart under the
immense crushing weight.
The hydrogen atoms are
stripped away, leaving
carbon atoms free to
bond with one another.
When carbon is subjected
to thousands of degrees
and enormous pressure,
what does it form?
It can form pure,
glittering crystalline
diamonds.
Laboratory experiments
on Earth, using high-powered
lasers and shockwave
compression, have replicated
similar conditions for
tiny fractions of a second.
The tests show that
hydrocarbons can break
apart and crystallize into
diamond under pressures
like those inside ice giants.
In the deep interior
of Neptune, scientists
suspect that diamonds may
be forming and precipitating
out of the hot,
dense fluid mantle.
They would drift downward
through the slush like
heavy hail falling toward
the planetary core.
As these diamond crystals
fall through the dense
mantle, they could generate
friction against the
surrounding slush, releasing
gravitational heat.
This exotic mechanism might
be one of the
secret power sources behind
why Neptune radiates so
much internal thermal energy.
Imagine a world where
storms of solid diamond
sink through a superheated
sea of liquid ice,
perhaps fueling the very
winds that howl thousands
of kilometers above.
Nature crafts solutions
that far outstrip the
wildest boundaries of human
imagination.
Scientists suspect this
may be one of
Neptune's secret power
sources.
